items.title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
items.abstract: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.

items.title: FinSafeGuard: A Quality-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Financial AI Safety
items.abstract: Generating high-quality synthetic datasets at scale remains a fundamental challenge for training specialized AI systems in data-scarce domains. We present a comprehensive methodology that produces 14.3 million quality-filtered synthetic training examples from a structured taxonomy of 632,000 scenario specifications. Our four-stage pipeline ad- dresses critical challenges in synthetic data quality, diversity, and realism through: (1) systematic pre-generation research establishing optimal generation parameters via diminishing returns analysis, (2) conditional auto evolution mechanisms that remediate low-diversity batches during generation, (3) a two-layer semantic deduplication architecture combining lexical and embedding-based methods, and (4) LLM-as-Judge quality evaluation filtering samples based on behavioral correctness and tuple fidelity. Empirical analysis across three domains (Banking, Insurance, Financial Services) demonstrates domain-specific deduplication patterns ranging from 9.9% to 40.6%, with output generation modes exhibiting highest redundancy. Our batch size optimization reveals mode-specific diversity saturation thresholds, enabling principled allocation strategies. The complete pipeline reduces 26.4M raw samples to 14.3M high-confidence examples through merge (20.9% reduction), semantic deduplication (18.7% reduction), and quality-based filtering (15.9% reduction), providing a reproducible framework for domain-specific synthetic data generation with rigorous quality control.

items.title: ForagerSim: Evaluating Embodied Map-Based Reasoning in Large-Scale Dynamic Worlds
items.abstract: Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces. In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all. Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning. To address this, we present ForagerSim --- an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas. ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks). We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods. Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.

items.title: FrameGRPO: Incentivizing Video Reasoning via Multi-Frame Rollouts and Temporal Credit
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.

items.abstract: FraudShield AI is a machine-learning project designed to identify potentially fraudulent credit card transactions using artificial intelligence. Built with Python, scikit-learn, pandas, and Streamlit, the application uses a Random Forest classification model to analyze transaction data and distinguish between legitimate and potentially fraudulent activity. It features an interactive dashboard for exploring transaction records, checking individual transactions, visualizing model performance, and examining feature importance. Through this project, I gained practical experience in machine learning, data analysis, model evaluation, and application development while exploring the challenges of imbalanced datasets and responsible AI. FraudShield AI reflects my interest in combining artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to develop practical solutions for financial security.

items.title: From Authorship to Accountability - Rethinking Copyright Governance for AI-Generated Art
items.abstract: This study examines how the rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) challenges traditional copyright law by shifting legal concerns beyond authorship and ownership toward transparency, disclosure, traceability, and accountability in AI-assisted artistic production.The study adopts a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology to analyse copyright principles, emerging regulatory frameworks, and policy developments relating to AI-generated content. Particular attention is given to the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, international copyright debates, and the Albanian legal framework under Law No. 35/2016 “On Copyright and Related Rights”.The analysis demonstrates that existing copyright regimes remain predominantly authorship-centred and provide limited guidance regarding accountability when AI systems contribute to artistic creation. Significant regulatory gaps persist concerning disclosure obligations, traceability of AI involvement, transparency of creative processes, and the allocation of responsibility among users, developers, and platform providers. The findings further indicate that accountabilitybased governance offers a valuable complement to traditional copyright doctrines in addressing the challenges of AI-assisted creativity. The study is limited to legal JUS & JUSTICIA No. 20, ISSUE 2/ 2026 95 and regulatory analysis and does not incorporate empirical evidence from creators, policymakers, technology developers, or judicial practice in Albania. Future research may benefit from examining stakeholder perspectives and the practical implementation of emerging AI governance frameworks. The findings support the development of governance mechanisms based on mandatory disclosure of AI involvement, documentation of human creative contribution, enhanced transparency standards, and traceability measures for AI-generated artistic content. These measures may strengthen legal certainty and improve copyright enforcement in AIassisted creative environments.The study contributes to current scholarship by moving beyond the traditional debate on authorship and copyrightability and proposing an accountability-oriented framework for copyright governance. It offers one of the first analyses linking transparency, disclosure, traceability, and accountability principles to the regulation of AI-generated art within both the Albanian and European legal contexts.

items.title: From Black Box to Controller: Inference-Time Steering of LLM via Feature Amplification
items.abstract: Inference-time steering is crucial for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications, where they must flexibly adjust behavior preferences. For instance, a model should dynamically adjust its caution level based on the risk of the scenario. This requirement introduces a challenge: modulating the intensity of LLM preferences. Prompt engineering can require task-specific prompt design, while fine-tuning requires additional optimization and data. These requirements can make repeated behavioral adjustments costly. To address this, we introduce NeuroSteer, a plug-and-play framework that enables flexible, quantitative adjustment of LLM preferences at inference time. NeuroSteer employs a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) as its controller. Comparing neuron activation frequencies between positive and negative examples isolates "feature neurons" that correspond to target preferences such as politeness and positive sentiment. During inference, the activations of selected SAE features are amplified in the latent representations to steer the output distribution. Users can adjust the strength of this steering on a per-scenario or per-user basis, granting the LLM fine-grained, quantifiable trait modulation. Our experiments show that NeuroSteer can alter sentiment, toxicity, stance, and politeness at inference time. It achieves higher target-direction steering scores than the compared baselines in several settings, with task- and strength-dependent trade-offs in generation quality.

items.title: From Chaos to Consistency: A Human-Centered Framework for AI-supported Assessment at a Mission-Driven Liberal Arts College
items.abstract: This practitioner inquiry reports on a pilot at a small Catholic liberal arts college that used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-supported tools to help faculty complete program-assessment documentation during a structured Education Day. Grounded in Catholic social teaching and human-centered AI principles, the pilot tested a framework organized around human judgment, ethical stewardship, and formative human-AI partnership. Survey results from the pilot cohort (N = 10; item-level valid responses varied) showed strong faculty endorsement, including unanimous agreement that the process deepened thinking about evidence of student learning and unanimous intent to use AI-supported tools in future cycles. Qualitative findings identified five themes: efficiency and cognitive scaffolding, human-in-the-loop validation, platform reliability and trust, data governance, and institutional support infrastructure. Findings suggest that mission-driven institutions can integrate AI into assessment responsibly when faculty formation, verification checkpoints, and governance structures precede broad implementation.

items.title: From Choice to Consequence: Active Resilience as the Value-Adding Extension of the Next? Path and Pattern of Personal and Business Innovation Practice
items.abstract: The research previously conducted by Benjamin and McLaughlin (2026) defined applied curiosity as the governing architecture for the transition from artificial intelligence (AI) to augmented understanding (AU), and presented cCC* (Curiosity opening Chances, discriminating Choices, authorising Changes) as its compact engine. That account stopped at authorisation. It did not address what happens when an authorised Change is enacted, meets resistance, produces an unintended consequence, or is overtaken by a shifting environment. Once change is enacted, subsequent Curiosity is enabled and thus the mechanism becomes recursive. This article develops active resilience (AR) as an extension of that research, serving as the architecture that governs that remainder and connecting Artificial Intelligence (AI), Applied Curiosity (AC), Augmented Understanding (AU) and Active Resilience (AR) into the sequence AI -> AC -> AU -> AR -> NEXT?: not the capacity to return to a prior state, but the capacity to enact a provisional best fit choice, detect its consequences, and use the resulting difference to reconstruct the next state. AR is defined against four guardrails: BBBB (the Belonging, Becoming, Bridging and Building movements applied at the point of action as a viability guardrail over bodily, behavioural, relational and environmental boundaries), FFFF (Form, Function, Frame and Future: whether an action responds to the form and function of the situation rather than merely to the frame placed over it, and what futures it opens or forecloses), the P-M-Theta-Phi test (practicable, methodically warranted, theoretically coherent, value explicit), and a feedback discipline that returns consequence to renewed curiosity rather than reinforcing the original construction. The framework is grounded in established literatures, including Holling's distinction between engineering and ecological resilience and his four-phase adaptive cycle of growth, conservation, release and reorganisation. Holling's work is particularly relevant to AR because it challenges the assumption that resilience is achieved by holding a system in a linear, stable state; attempts to suppress variability and maintain tight control can instead reduce adaptive capacity, accumulate fragility and increase the probability of eventual system disruption. AR also draws on Argyris and Schon's account of single-loop and double-loop organisational learning, Weick's concept of enactment, and von Bertalanffy's general systems account of equifinality. Within this literature, cCC* is positioned as an operational synthesis: a repeatable mechanism for translating these principles into the ongoing processes of inquiry, discrimination, action and adaptation. It extends the R1-R16 transitional register introduced previously, reading it this time as an architecture of choice under AEIOUF (Agency, Environment, Identity, Options, Understanding, Futures). A conceptual method for AR enactment and sixteen accompanying research propositions are offered for organisational strategy, stakeholder engagement, public narrative and reflective governance. The central claim is that an AU relationship is not complete at the moment a decision is authorised. It is complete only when the organisation or person can act on that decision, absorb what the action reveals, and remain capable of choosing again. MORE, in this account, is not a state reached once but a capacity kept renewable.

items.title: From chronic kidney disease classification to genuine early prediction: a systematic review of artificial intelligence, methodological quality, and translational evidence
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence has been widely applied to chronic kidney disease (CKD), but the term ‘prediction” is frequently used for tasks ranging from contemporaneous disease classification to genuine forecasting of future renal outcomes. This systematic review examined this distinction while evaluating methodological quality and evidence for clinical translation. Methods A predefined Scopus-based search covering 2021–2026 identified eligible AI- and machine-learning-based CKD studies. After screening and duplicate reconciliation, 169 unique primary studies were included. Future-oriented prediction required an identifiable baseline, predictors available at or before baseline, a subsequent renal outcome, and a meaningful prediction horizon. Studies were evaluated for modeling approaches, datasets, validation, calibration, explainability, clinical usefulness, and methodological quality using PROBAST+AI. Results Of 169 studies, 122 (72.2%) addressed current-state CKD detection or classification, while only 46 (27.2%) contained a clearly future-oriented prediction component. Seventeen studies used geographic or institutional external validation and only four used an independent external cohort or dataset. Calibration was assessed in 12 studies and explicit explainability methods were reported in 16. PROBAST+AI identified high overall risk of bias in 156 studies during development and 164 during evaluation, with no study achieving an overall low-risk judgement. Discussion CKD-AI evidence is substantially stronger for retrospective classification than for genuine early prediction or clinical translation. Future research should prioritize longitudinal prediction, independent and temporal validation, leakage-resistant analysis, calibration, clinically validated explainability, and prospective real-world evaluation.

items.title: From Cities to Distributed Intelligence Landscapes: Hybrid Foresight Through Drawing, Philosophy, and Generative AI
items.abstract: This research investigates an alternative approach to long-range urban foresight by employing a hybrid methodology combining deep-time conceptual reflection, exploratory drawing as an epistemic practice, structured interpretative analysis, and AI-assisted dialogical synthesis. The resulting synthesis articulates a theoretically generated post-urban scenario characterized by dispersed human habitation embedded in ecological landscapes, supported by advanced digital connectivity and artificial intelligence. Technologically intensive functions remain concentrated in infrastructural hubs, while everyday life becomes integrated with natural environments through walking-based mobility, bio-inspired architecture, and multispecies coexistence. The proposed model reinterprets urbanity as distributed intelligence within ecological continuity.

items.title: From Co-Presence to Willingness to Pay More: How Remote Guidance Service and Embodied Action Simulation Drive Brand Value in the Virtual Environments
items.abstract: This study investigates how perceived co-presence contributes to brand value in virtual service environments. Drawing on Mirror Neuron Theory and Embodied Knowledge Theory, we propose embodied action simulation as an indirect path linking perceived co-presence to brand image and subsequent willingness to pay more. We further conceptualize remote guidance service as a service-design boundary condition and compare AI- versus human-delivered guidance from a task-agent fit perspective. Three studies (two laboratory studies in Roblox Vans World and a field survey of smart fitness mirror users) support the framework. Embodied action simulation mediates the relationship between perceived co-presence and brand image, while this indirect association is stronger when remote guidance service is present. A stronger indirect association is also observed among AI-coach than human-coach users in procedural, task-oriented service contexts, consistent with task-agent fit. These findings clarify how social presence relates to embodied participation, brand value creation, and consumers’ willingness to pay more.

items.title: From few‐shot learning to data‐efficient intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Modern artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved remarkable progress by scaling data, model size, and computation. Yet scaling alone does not resolve one of the most fundamental gaps between machine and human intelligence: the ability to learn, adapt, and act from limited experience. This limitation is especially visible when labeled examples, expert feedback, user interactions, or real‐world trials are scarce, costly, or dynamically changing. Humans can often grasp a new concept, adapt to a new goal, or personalize behavior after only a few examples or interactions, but many AI systems remain fragile under the same conditions. My research studies data‐efficient generalization: how learning systems can acquire useful priors, adapt to new tasks, and reuse limited experience under bounded supervision. In this article, I trace a continuous research path from few‐shot learning to meta‐learning, in‐context learning, and data‐efficient agentic learning. I first revisit few‐shot learning as a foundational problem and explain how data‐, model‐, and algorithm‐level priors make learning possible when empirical risk minimization is unreliable. I then describe our work on meta‐learning, where task‐level information and parameter‐efficient adaptation enable fast generalization. Next, I discuss in‐context learning in large language models (LLMs) as an implicit form of learning to learn, and show how its connection to classical meta‐learning provides both theoretical insight and practical guidance. Finally, I turn to large language model (LLM)‐based agents, where data efficiency expands beyond labels to include demonstrations, reasoning traces, tool‐use records, preferences, memory, and feedback. Across AI for science, biomedical knowledge discovery, recommendation, search, and personalization, the common thread is simple: more capable AI should extract more learning signal from less experience.

items.title: From GEMBA to GPT: Artificial Intelligence for the Medical Office Assistant
items.abstract: Administrative tasks by medical office staff are a significant but underappreciated driver of delayed patient care, staff burnout, and escalating operational costs in modern urology practice. A forced Gemba Walk in front-desk responsibilities exposed many previously invisible inefficiencies in my own practice, specifically the workflow with regard to faxes and patient phone calls. These tasks are high-volume, redundant, and time-consuming—making them an ideal task for artificial intelligence (AI). Large language models (LLM) can integrate with electronic medical record (EMR) platforms to automate these repetitive tasks. For example, optical character recognition (OCR) can be used to transform incoming faxed images to operational datapoints. The models can then automatically classify the document, sort the file directly to patient charts, and clinically triage referrals and results by urgency. Furthermore, AI voice agents or AI receptionists can handle routine phone calls with full EMR integration and documentation, while complex cases can be escalated to human staff. In an era of increasing burnout, transitioning from manual workflows to an AI-augmented paradigm allows providers to work at the top of their scope. These operational efficiencies carry broader health policy implications, including shortened referral-to-consultation intervals for urgent diagnoses, improved patient care and communication, and the generation of structured analytics to drive system-level quality improvement.

items.title: From Heuristics to Learning a Review of AI Methods for Logic Gate in EDA
items.abstract: Description This review paper examines how Artificial Intelligence is changing logic gate synthesis in Electronic Design Automation (EDA). Classical heuristics such as Karnaugh maps, Quine-McCluskey and AIG rewriting struggle to scale to circuits with billions of gates, especially when balancing power, performance and area (PPA). The paper builds on Astillero's study of AI-driven synthesis and organizes the field around three model families: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs): these represent circuits as directed graphs and estimate delay, power and congestion before physical routing. Reinforcement Learning (RL): agents learn sequences of rewrite operations on And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and Majority-Inverter Graphs (MIGs) that greedy optimizers miss, guided by a combined area, delay and power reward. Large Circuit Models (LCMs): transformer models that translate specifications or HDL directly into gate-level netlists. The paper compares these methods with traditional flows across five dimensions: optimization strategy, PPA exploration, scaling, parasitic awareness and adaptability across technology libraries. It then covers three applications: approximate computing, SAT sweeping and equivalence checking, and automated CPU/ASIC generation. It concludes that data scarcity and the lack of guaranteed functional correctness are the main barriers to adoption. It argues that closing the loop between generation and formal verification is the key research priority.

items.title: From innovation to implementation: a global scoping review of artificial intelligence applications, governance, and challenges in humanitarian contexts
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool for supporting humanitarian action through hazards and crisis prediction, real time monitoring of evolving crisis conditions and humanitarian needs, resource allocation, and decision-making. However, evidence on how AI is implemented, evaluated, and governed across humanitarian contexts remains fragmented. In this scoping review, we mapped the global evidence on the application of AI in humanitarian settings, including its distribution across the emergency management cycle, deployment maturity, and evaluation. We also identified any governance considerations, as well as enabling factors for and challenges to its implementation, with particular attention to the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, Gulf Cooperation Council countries (GCC), and Qatar. Methods: The methodology of this scoping review followed the framework set by Arksey and O'Malley, which comprises the formulation of the research question, selection of records, data charting, and synthesis of findings. We searched six databases (ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus), queried Google Scholar, and ran targeted grey literature searches through the webpages of major humanitarian organisations for records reporting on the application, implementation, or governance of AI in humanitarian contexts. We descriptively and narratively synthesised the extracted data. Results: We included 57 scholarly publications and 17 grey literature reports. Application of AI was most frequently reported in sudden-onset natural disasters, particularly floods and earthquakes, and was commonly used to support disaster monitoring, crisis informatics, search-and-rescue, logistics optimisation, hazard prediction, and geospatial analysis. Deep learning and machine learning were the most common model families. Across the emergency management cycle, most applications of AI focused on preparedness and response, while recovery was rarely addressed. Geographically, most evidence originated from Asia, while research from the MENA and GCC regions remained limited. Most reported systems remained prototypes or retrospectively validated models, with relatively few seeing operational deployment or field implementation. Governance issues were discussed more extensively in grey literature than in scholarly publications. Community participation, equity considerations, and formal governance frameworks were inconsistently reported. Conclusions: AI is increasingly being applied in humanitarian contexts, but it is heterogeneously distributed across regions, humanitarian contexts, and emergency management. Greater emphasis is needed on real-world deployment, implementation-focused evaluation, participatory approaches, and governance frameworks that support responsible, equitable, and context-sensitive AI adoption.

items.title: From Personal Superinformation to Next?: Hyperpersonalisation as an Architecture of Human Agency, Choice, Consequence and Recursive Consciousing
items.abstract: On a Monday morning a chief executive unlocks her phone. Over the weekend the agent has read the emails, moved two meetings, drafted three replies, booked a flight and held one sensitive action for approval. Everything worked. Nothing failed. And somewhere in the smoothness of it, one thing went quiet: it is no longer easy to say which of those decisions she actually chose. That seamlessness is the landscape Meta's 2025-2026 personal-superintelligence programme now occupies - an agent that understands a person, remembers context, connects to services, plans, acts, requests permission and exposes an audit trail. These are substantial capabilities. What they leave structurally unsettled is the logically prior question: how a person's goals are formed, contested, revised, related to OTHER people, converted into choices, exposed to consequence, and recursively reconstructed after action. The Benjamin et al. research programme addresses that prior question, and its evidentiary spine precedes the present debate: strategic decision freedom and opportunity construction (Benjamin & Béchervaise, 2007); responsibility and socially sustainable enterprise (Béchervaise & Benjamin, 2013); relational meaning and POETRY/ARMS (Benjamin, Bitetto & Sharma, 2022); differentiated responses to emergent technologies (Benjamin & Bitetto, 2023); behavioural-economic differentiation using large population datasets (Benjamin, Bitetto & Bound, 2024); and the 2026 cCC*, AEIOUF and sixteen-state Architecture of Choice publications. The 2026 publications formalise consciousing as a recursive movement through chances, choices and maintained changes, reporting a bounded sixteen-position coordinate architecture using Roy Morgan Single Source data. The resulting argument is architectural and empirically testable: computational capacity becomes humanly consequential only when converted through situated inquiry, alternative construction, perspective differentiation, authorised choice, action, consequence and recursive return. That progression is AI→AC→AU→AR→IC. NEXT? is the generative hinge R16(g)→R1(g+1), where experienced consequence changes the question, criteria, relationship or identity that begins the next cycle. Hyperpersonalisation is therefore defined not as perfect prediction of a person, but as high-fidelity support for the person-in-relation to construct and reconstruct a Question-in-Context while retaining authorship of choice. The monograph converts that proposition into an R1-R16 operating protocol, an AEIOUF/SELF↔OTHER audit, a distinction between targeting and agency, and a falsifiable research agenda. Its conclusion: Meta's trajectory may become a powerful substrate for NEXT?, but computational power, persistent memory and autonomous execution are not substitutes for consciousing. The strategic opening is a human-AI relation that makes changing questions, alternatives, reasons, permissions, consequences and future commitments more visible, contestable and auditable.

items.title: From TCP/IP to MCP: Security and Governance Lessons from Internet Protocols for Agentic AI
items.abstract: The past two years have seen considerable interest in protocols for managing how AI agents interact with human users, external tools, and each other. In many ways, these protocols, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A), mirror the suite of protocols that underlie the modern internet. Motivated by this parallel, this paper draws lessons from the development, history, and governance of internet protocols with the aim of informing the responsible development of AI agent protocols. Based on our analysis, we make two conclusions. First, if AI agent protocols do not sufficiently prioritise security in the early stages of development, they risk accumulating a security deficit that becomes increasingly costly to address over time due to practical and economic challenges. Second, current governance structures for AI agent protocols centralise decision-making power in a small number of individuals and companies, raising important questions regarding legitimacy, especially if they become critical digital infrastructure. We conclude with a discussion and implications for policymakers and developers of AI agent protocols.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: From Verbal Attribution to Internal Measurement A Cross-System Framework for Comparing Human Brain and Artificial Intelligence Responses to External Stimuli
items.abstract: Abstract Public discussions about whether artificial intelligence possesses emotions, subjective experience, or even consciousness often rely on linguistic output, behavioral performance, and observers’ judgments. An AI system’s ability to describe its own state is not, by itself, sufficient to demonstrate subjective experience. At the same time, the fact that an AI system is non-biological does not by itself justify the conclusion that it lacks all forms of subjective experience. This paper proposes a cross-system experimental framework. When humans and artificial intelligence systems are exposed to functionally corresponding external stimuli, researchers can record brain activity in humans and internal states in AI systems, then compare how the stimuli alter internal processing and how those changes affect subsequent judgments and behavior. The goal is not to require AI systems to reproduce the structure, waveforms, or numerical values of the human brain, but to identify response relationships that can survive repeated testing and causal examination. Such comparison cannot be achieved merely by converting two kinds of data into the same format. Researchers must first establish what candidate measures mean within each system, then construct possible cross-system correspondences and test whether those correspondences can predict changes under new materials and new conditions. Only when a proposed relationship does more than describe existing results, and instead generates successful new predictions, is there stronger reason to discuss whether the two systems may share some common processing principle. Using “violation of an acquired expectation” as an example, this paper illustrates how the framework could be translated into an initial research program. It also distinguishes transient computational states, states maintained within context, and persistent states across sessions, and discusses long-term interaction, consciousness-relevant human controls, internal intervention, and statistical confounds. This paper is a conceptual and methodological proposal. It does not provide an already validated test for consciousness, nor does it claim to have solved all technical problems of cross-system comparison. Even if the results ultimately fail to support the presence of subjective experience in artificial intelligence, data linking external conditions, internal states, and subsequent behavior may still be useful for model evaluation, training, and interaction design.

items.title: Fusion of TimeSHAP and Anchors: Towards Stable and Coherent Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Botnet Detection in the Internet of Things
items.abstract: Deep learning-based IoT botnet detection has reached high predictive performance; however, its practical deployment remains constrained by the lack of operationally actionable explainability. This paper introduces TimeAnchor, a hybrid explainability framework that integrates TimeSHAP and Anchors to enhance the temporal stability and internal consistency of explanations while preserving acceptable fidelity. The approach is evaluated on two complementary datasets: CICIDS2017, reflecting controlled and structured traffic conditions, and IoT-23, characterised by real-world, noisy, and highly heterogeneous attack scenarios. The results indicate that TimeAnchor substantially improves explanation consistency and stability across both corpora, achieving high coherence on CICIDS2017 and yielding average gains in stability and consistency on IoT-23 compared with the individual methods. These improvements are accompanied by a moderate trade-off in local fidelity, which appears acceptable given the overall enhancement in explanatory robustness. These findings support the relevance of TimeAnchor for explainable IoT botnet detection in dynamic and realistic operational environments.

items.title: Future Directions in Fuzzy Decision-Making and Risk Management
items.abstract: In an era defined by intensifying uncertainties, spanning geopolitical tensions, climate variability, pandemics and global supply chain disruption, fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making (FMCDM) has emerged as a critical paradigm for robust risk assessment and mitigation. This chapter presents a comprehensive review of recent advances in FMCDM from 2021 to 2025, synthesizing insights from over 400 studies across sectors such as healthcare, engineering and sustainable operations. Key developments include the rapid growth of hybrid fuzzy models integrating interval type-2 fuzzy sets with methods like TOPSIS, DEMATEL and BWM, as well as the evolution of enriched fuzzy extensions (e.g., Fermatean and T-spherical sets) to address complex, multi-dimensional vagueness. Persistent issues such as computational scalability, inconsistencies in expert judgements and the challenges of modelling epistemic uncertainty are critically examined. Empirical evidence highlights applications such as fuzzy-enhanced healthcare risk matrices, which improve transparency by up to 30% through probabilistic membership functions. The chapter identifies emerging directions involving the fusion of FMCDM with artificial intelligence, machine learning, big-data analytics and blockchain to enable real-time, adaptive and secure decision environments. By bridging theoretical advancements with practical implementations, this chapter offers actionable insights for designing resilient, uncertainty-aware risk governance frameworks in an increasingly volatile global context.

items.title: Future trends and challenges in medical tourism: Precision medicine, digital infrastructure, sustainability, and the shift from volume to value
items.abstract: The evolution of medical tourism is increasingly characterised by a shift from isolated, procedure-based journeys to complex, transnational care pathways supported by digital innovation and changing patient values. As technological advances—including genomics, artificial intelligence, and telemedicine—reshape the organisation of care, the industry faces a dual challenge: harnessing innovation to improve patient outcomes while addressing urgent concerns about equity, sustainability, and data governance. This chapter explores the future trends and systemic challenges shaping the next phase of cross-border care. It examines the rise of personalised and precision medicine, highlighting how genomic testing and targeted therapies enable customised treatment while raising new ethical questions. It considers the rapid expansion of wellness and mental health tourism, emphasising evidence-based, integrative models that balance clinical rigour with environmental sustainability. A central focus is digital infrastructure and trust—assessing how AI, remote monitoring, and blockchain can create safer, “tele-first” pathways that lower carbon footprints and enhance continuity of care. By addressing fragmented accountability and the risk of widening health inequalities, the chapter concludes that the future of medical tourism depends on a value-driven approach where destinations differentiate themselves through transparency, ethical governance, and a genuine commitment to the well-being of both patients and local communities.

items.title: GAIDA: Generative AI for Human-in-the-Loop Document Annotation
items.abstract: Document annotation is a fundamental yet labor-intensive step in building document information extraction systems. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate parts of this process, we argue that annotation systems should be judged not by how completely they remove human effort, but by how effectively they redirect it toward review and correction. We propose a modular human-in-the-loop architecture that integrates OCR-based extraction, LLM-based semantic pre-annotation, and human validation in a single editable workflow, and present \textbf{GAIDA}, a research prototype serving as its reference implementation. GAIDA supports interchangeable OCR engines, LLM backends, and prompt configurations, and enables stage-specific measurement of annotation effort. In an initial single-annotator, stage-specific study on the FUNSD scanned-form and WildReceipt retail-receipt benchmarks, OCR assistance reduced region-creation and transcription time by up to \textbf{80.9\%}, and reviewing LLM pre-annotations reduced semantic-labeling time by up to \textbf{73.7\%}, despite imperfect pre-annotations of 78.86\% and 86.98\% Micro F1 on FUNSD and WildReceipt, respectively. Finally, we reuse the same implementation, adapting only OCR and prompt configuration, to build and openly release \textbf{AraReceipt}, a manually annotated dataset of 100 Arabic receipt images labeled with 25 key-information classes. The results indicate that imperfect automated outputs provide practical value when presented as editable suggestions under human control.

items.title: GAME-BASED LEARNING WITH AI TO MAINTAIN THE RIGHT BALANCE
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into game-based learning (GBL) offers adaptive, personalized, and engaging experiences for early language education. AI-powered games can enhance vocabulary, listening comprehension, and speaking confidence through real-time feedback and adaptive difficulty, but raise questions about balancing AI guidance, parental involvement, and child autonomy. Drawing on GBL theory, flow theory, and the input hypothesis, this paper identifies four dimensions of balance—pedagogical, parental involvement, engagement, and child autonomy—and proposes research questions and a conceptual framework for AI-supported game-based microlearning systems for English acquisition among children aged 5–8.

items.title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
items.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio-visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention-based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task-stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature- and logit-level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio-visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM-CIL.

items.title: Generative AI Continuance in Turkish Higher Education: A Mixed Methods Study
items.abstract: The study draws on two complementary data sources. The quantitative data come from a cross-sectional online survey administered to university students enrolled in Turkish higher education institutions. Stratified random sampling ensures representation across institutional types. The strata include metropolitan foundation universities, metropolitan public universities, and provincial state universities. The survey instrument uses validated scales adapted from prior research on Technology Continuance Theory and GenAI adoption. All items are measured on a five-point Likert scale. The constructs measured include Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Confirmation, Satisfaction, Trust, Perceived Security, Continuance Intention, and Use. Trust items measure confidence in the AI tools. One item asks whether students trust GenAI tools to provide accurate information. Another asks whether students trust developers to prevent unethical use of student data. The survey does not measure trust in university administration. The survey is available in Turkish and English. Translation follows a rigorous protocol. The research team drafts the survey in English, translates it into Turkish, and back-translates it into English. Native speakers review both versions for clarity, cultural accuracy, and linguistic equivalence.The qualitative data come from semi-structured interviews with academics. Purposive sampling recruits academics across three institutional strata. The strata are elite foundation universities in Istanbul, major public universities in Ankara, and provincial state universities in eastern and southeastern Türkiye. The sample also includes academics from Northern Cyprus, transnational institutions, and the Turkish and Kurdish diaspora. The interview protocol explores GenAI use in teaching and research, perceptions of institutional support, experiences with infrastructure limitations, views on domestic AI models, and intentions regarding academic migration. The protocol includes specific probes for Kurdish academics and academics at conservative foundation universities. The interview guide is drafted in English and translated into Turkish and Kurdish. Native speakers review both translations. Back-translation ensures linguistic equivalence. Interviews are conducted in Turkish, Kurdish, or English based on participant preference. Interviews are audio-recorded with participant consent and transcribed verbatim.Data analysis uses Generalized Structured Component Analysis in SmartPLS 4.0 for the quantitative phase. Preliminary data screening uses SPSS 28. Screening includes tests for normality, multicollinearity, and common method bias. The qualitative phase uses WEBQDA for digital coding. The coding framework includes deductive codes from Technology Continuance Theory and inductive codes that emerge from the data. Deductive codes include Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Satisfaction, Trust in AI tools, Perceived Security, and Continuance Intention. Inductive codes include Institutional Trust, Infrastructure Context, Diaspora and Academic Retention, and Domestic AI Sovereignty. The research team builds a code co-occurrence matrix to trace links between institutional trust and trust in AI tools.Ethical approval comes from the Ethics Committee of CEOS.PP at the Polytechnic Institute of Porto. Data collection follows the Turkish Personal Data Protection Law and the General Data Protection Regulation. Participants receive information sheets and provide written informed consent. All data are anonymised upon collection. Participants receive alphanumeric codes that indicate region and institutional type but do not reveal individual identities. Audio recordings are deleted after transcription. Transcripts are stored on an encrypted, password-protected server accessible only to the research team. Data are retained for five years and then permanently deleted.

items.title: Generative AI in University Mathematics Education Using the Theory–Context–Methodology Framework: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Advances in generative AI are opening new opportunities for mathematics learning in higher education, but systematic mapping of the Theory–Context–Methodology (TCM) framework to integrate generative AI into mathematics learning remains limited. This study aims to identify the theories or conceptual frameworks, application contexts, and research methods used in studies of generative AI in higher education mathematics education. The method used is a PRISMA-based systematic literature review. The search was conducted on Scopus, Lens, and Dimensions, yielding 322 initial articles; after deduplication, screening, and eligibility assessment, 31 articles were analyzed. Article quality was assessed using the MMAT, while data were analyzed through TCM-based coding. The results indicate that generative AI is conceptualized as a pedagogical tool, a technology adoption, pedagogical competence, mathematical activity, and a cognitive partner. Its application is dominant in the classroom, general mathematics, ChatGPT, and for conceptual understanding. Methodologically, the studies were dominated by qualitative and quantitative approaches, while mixed methods and R&D/development research remained limited. These findings underscore the need for AI-based instructional designs that are critical, ethical, and supported by more integrative empirical research.

items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Higher Education: Applications, Challenges, Ethical Concerns, and Future Directions explores the growing role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) in transforming higher education. The book examines their applications in teaching, learning, research, academic writing, assessment, and personalized education. It highlights how AI-powered tools can support educators, enhance student engagement, improve access to learning resources, and facilitate academic productivity. At the same time, it addresses key challenges, including academic dishonesty, data privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, and the potential overdependence on AI-generated content. The book also discusses ethical considerations, institutional policies, responsible AI use, and the importance of maintaining human judgment in educational practices. Furthermore, it explores future directions, emerging technologies, and strategies for integrating AI into higher education effectively. This book is a valuable resource for educators, researchers, students, academic administrators, and policymakers interested in understanding and responsibly adopting AI-driven educational innovations.

The book examines their applications in teaching, learning, research, academic writing, assessment, and personalized education. It highlights how AI-powered tools can support educators, enhance student engagement, improve access to learning resources, and facilitate academic productivity. At the same time, it addresses key challenges, including academic dishonesty, data privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, and the potential overdependence on AI-generated content. The book also discusses ethical considerations, institutional policies, responsible AI use, and the importance of maintaining human judgment in educational practices. Furthermore, it explores future directions, emerging technologies, and strategies for integrating AI into higher education effectively. This book is a valuable resource for educators, researchers, students, academic administrators, and policymakers interested in understanding and responsibly adopting AI-driven educational innovations.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in education mapping research trends and future directions
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) recently appeared as an issue of its time which has been changing the educational landscape at a considerable rate and opening new pathways and challenges for educators and learners. Therefore, in terms of GenAI for education this bibliometric analysis will characterize the change and development by mapping trends and patterns, examining prevalent subject areas in academia interest. Following the established criteria, we ran a systematic search on Scopus database with the identification and analysis of 121 peer-reviewed documents (journal articles, review articles and conference papers; selection reported with reference to the PRISMA 2020 guideline) published between January 2023 and March 2025 related to GenAI applied in education. The thematic labels attached to the algorithmically generated VOSviewer clusters were assigned by the researchers, and interpretations of regional patterns are presented as tentative. The article features papers discussing ways to use GenAI in learner-centered teaching, curriculum development and assessment. The findings reveal a rapid increase in research output between 2023 (23 articles) and 2024 (67 articles), followed by 31 articles in the first quarter of 2025, and substantial international collaboration (34% of the articles). Moreover, the thematic analysis shows that pedagogical integration and instructional design (55.4% of the articles), assessment and academic integrity (44.6%) and ethical and societal implications (39.7%) are the most prominent themes, with a shift from ethical and assessment concerns in 2023 towards pedagogical integration and learning outcomes in 2024-2025. Research affiliated with the United States, the United Kingdom, China and Germany dominates the corpus, whereas research from Latin America and Africa appears under-represented. The review proposes future directions of research and spells out an array of issues that have until now gone unexamined by helping the reader enter the intellectual landscape of GenAI in education. The bibliometric evidence indicates growing scholarly attention to the potential of GenAI in education; this study did not appraise the quality of the evidence on learning outcomes. Nonetheless, designers are being asked to collectively conduct further research to address any potential negative effects of the technology, and create useful design frameworks, to implement this technology into the education system worldwide, without compromising on justice and morality.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Language and Literary Studies: A Systematic Review of Applications, Ethical Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming language and literary studies by introducing new approaches to language learning, writing, translation, textual interpretation, literary analysis, and creative production. Powered by large language models and other generative technologies, these systems can generate and revise texts, summarize complex literary works, identify linguistic patterns, support multilingual communication, and facilitate interactive learning. However, their growing adoption raises important concerns regarding authorship, academic integrity, linguistic bias, cultural representation, interpretive reliability, data privacy, and the potential marginalization of less-resourced languages and literary traditions. This systematic review examines the applications, ethical challenges, and future directions of GenAI in language and literary studies. It adopts a structured literature-review approach to synthesize research on educational applications, computational linguistics, translation, literary interpretation, creative writing, and digital humanities. The review organizes the literature around five major themes: language learning and teaching, academic and creative writing, translation and multilingual communication, literary analysis and interpretation, and ethical and institutional governance. The synthesis suggests that GenAI can expand access to language-learning support, facilitate text-based research, improve writing processes, and support new forms of literary experimentation. Nevertheless, its effectiveness depends on human oversight, contextual accuracy, critical evaluation, and sensitivity to linguistic and cultural diversity. The review further identifies continuing challenges associated with fabricated information, algorithmic bias, unclear intellectual-property arrangements, overreliance on automated assistance, and inadequate representation of minority languages. It argues that GenAI should complement rather than replace human linguistic judgment, literary expertise, and creative agency. Future research should prioritize transparent evaluation frameworks, culturally responsive models, multilingual equity, responsible pedagogical integration, and interdisciplinary collaboration. The review contributes an integrated perspective for researchers, educators, writers, and institutions seeking to use generative technologies responsibly in language and literary scholarship.

items.title: Geometric Diagnostics for Continuous Style Control in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Explicit ratio prompts can request intermediate writing styles, but endpoint classification does not reveal proportional responses at internal ratios. We present a geometric protocol using model-specific endpoints and shared references in external sentence-embedding spaces. It excludes mechanically perfect endpoints from primary errors, retains unclipped projections, and separates axial calibration error from normalized off-axis drift. StyleBlend-Bench contains eight style axes and 320 scenarios. Five Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 checkpoints generated 33,600 texts over seven ratios and three seeds; three encoders produced 100,800 geometric records. An external GPT generator adds 6719 usable texts. A full five-model prompt-by-temperature experiment contains 95,994 usable condition records. Shared-reference BGE-M3 calibration error ranges from 0.176 to 0.212; other encoder/reference choices change model ordering. Two automatic evaluators correlate strongly in style intensity (r = 0.910), but content-pass agreement is 76.2%. The trajectories were rarely one-dimensional: first-component variance ranged from 0.349 to 0.408 and ordered path-length ratios from 4.64 to 5.20. The protocol diagnoses model response under specified anchors and encoders; it does not establish a human perceptual scale or absolute cross-model style coordinate.

items.title: GeoTrain: Energy-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Foundation Model Training on Heterogeneous Geo-Distributed Resources
items.abstract: Training foundation models at the frontier typically requires large-scale dedicated and centralized clusters with fast interconnects - infrastructure that is prohibitively expensive and generally accessible only to well-resourced organizations. Decentralized training over pooled, geographically distributed GPUs offers an alternative, but introduces substantial heterogeneity in compute, memory, power, and network performance. Existing distributed training systems are primarily designed for clusters with fast, low-latency interconnects and typically use all available GPUs when configuring parallel training. In geo-distributed environments, however, slower devices and weak network links can become bottlenecks, while optimizing solely for throughput overlooks significant energy cost. We present GeoTrain, an automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes training performance and energy consumption for heterogeneous geo-distributed GPU environments. GeoTrain simultaneously selects GPUs, partitions model layers, and determines pipeline configurations while accounting for heterogeneous compute, memory, power, and network constraints. To efficiently explore this large combinatorial search space, GeoTrain employs an optimized memetic algorithm with specialized genetic operators and local search. Experiments with decoder-only Transformer models on real-world and simulated heterogeneous topologies demonstrate that GeoTrain reduces iteration time and energy consumption by up to $61.4\%$ and $11.7\%$, respectively, over the existing state-of-the-art approaches. It also finds the exact optimum on verifiable instances and scales beyond exact methods as the number of GPUs increases, while exposing favorable energy-time trade-offs, including cases where its time-optimal distributed training plan is both faster and more energy-efficient than the baselines.

items.title: Getting Perspectives on Quality in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Research Software Engineering (RSEng) is grounded in the belief that better, higher-quality software enables better research. As we look to the future of RSEng, we see that generative AI could substantially accelerate and expand the scope of research software development, but it also fundamentally shifts the nature of research software development by making code easier to generate than to understand, validate, or maintain. This is especially consequential in scientific computing, where software quality is directly tied to reproducibility, trust, and scientific validity. For RSEs, there is now an urgent need to advance a practical vision for how we will succeed in producing high-quality, trustworthy software under these new circumstances. We argue that in the age of AI for science, developers play an essential role in creating quality by reasoning about, negotiating, and ensuring it across the software lifecycle. We advance a theory that helps explain what, exactly, developers contribute by focusing on three constructs: values, which shape which quality attributes matter; expertise, which enables individuals to pursue and evaluate those attributes; and collaboration, which coordinates diverse forms of knowledge and accountability. To both build better AI tools for research software development and prepare our workforce, we need to better understand which values, what kinds of expertise, and what forms of collaboration will prove most helpful. For that, we seek expert input from Research Software Engineers(RSEs). This poster provides participants with an entertaining, interactive experience with the core ideas of our research. As well as sharing the preliminary thoughts and opinions gathered from an interview study that is currently underway. This interview study was motivated by the work this poster is highlighting. By showing the preliminary results we hope to initiate a dialog with RSEs. As such invite the audience to reflect on what quality means in their own practice, and the work that is needed to achieve it in concert with AI. Attendees can contribute responses on post-it notes attached to the poster and will be invited to continue the conversation through a survey. We will encourage those who wish to learn more about our team’s ongoing work on these topics to attend our talk "We Create Quality: Towards a Human-Centric Theory of Research Software Quality in the Age of AI”.

items.title: Global research trends in aged care facilities management (ACFM): a scoping review and bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to map global research trends in aged care facilities management (ACFM) and identify thematic gaps to inform future practice and policy. Design/methodology/approach A scoping review and bibliometric analysis were conducted using the Scopus database, extracting 454 peer-reviewed articles (1980–2024) from 173 journals. The review followed preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, while VOSviewer and Biblioshiny were applied to analyse co-authorship, co-citation, keyword networks and thematic evolution. Findings Three thematic clusters dominate the field: assistive technologies for digital health monitoring, safety and autonomy; integrated care systems embedded in physical environments to deliver person-centred services; and community-based infrastructures that support ageing-in-place. Despite growth in publications, gaps remain in linking facilities management with sociotechnical and gerontological perspectives, limiting integration of digital innovations and interdisciplinary frameworks. Practical implications The findings highlight actionable strategies for policymakers, designers and facility managers to integrate technology, spatial design and community services, enabling more inclusive and resilient aged care environments. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first combined scoping review and bibliometric analysis of ACFM. It positions facilities management (FM) as a critical driver in addressing ageing challenges and advancing inclusive, technology-enabled care.

items.title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
items.abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not transfer reliably: conditioned on safe English completions, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%. Bypass risk concentrates in a subset of language families, a pattern broadly shared across models. The shared ordering is confounded with translation degeneracy, but its variation across models is significant and survives every control we apply. We also show that per-model bypass rates do not identify a stable ranking: nine of ten models change rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity, with no change to any underlying response.

items.title: Global trends and research patterns of digital health and telemedicine innovation in public healthcare organizations: A bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the development, research trends, and intellectual structure of health service innovation in public sector organizations through a comprehensive bibliometric approach. This investigation is particularly timely in response to the escalating global demand for effective healthcare delivery and the transformative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on institutional frameworks. Despite the rapidly growing body of literature concerning public health management, comprehensive bibliometric studies that systematically map the specific intersection of "innovation" and "public sector healthcare" remain notably limited. To address this gap, this study employs a quantitative bibliometric methodology, analyzing 379 high-quality documents retrieved from the Scopus database after a rigorous multi-stage filtering process to ensure data relevance and academic rigor. The analytical framework combines performance analysis with advanced science mapping techniques, including co-occurrence (co-word) analysis and bibliographic coupling. VOSviewer software was utilized for network visualization and thematic clustering to identify the underlying intellectual linkages. The results demonstrate a significant and exponential increase in publications after 2019, underscoring a shift in global research priorities. Dominant keywords identified include telemedicine, human factors, healthcare delivery systems, and public hospital management. The analysis further delineates four key thematic clusters: digital health transformation, clinical and demographic studies, public healthcare service optimization, and pandemic-driven crisis innovation. These findings highlight the critical role of COVID-19 as a catalyst in accelerating the adoption of disruptive technologies. The study emphasizes that for public sector organizations to remain resilient, there is an urgent need to strengthen digital health infrastructure and implement adaptive governance models that can accommodate rapid technological shifts. Ultimately, this research provides a structured mapping of thematic evolution and intellectual linkages, offering a strategic roadmap for policymakers and scholars to identify under-researched areas and prioritize future interventions in health service innovation.

items.title: GPT-6 Astra Is a Native Visuo-Tactile Policy for Contact-Rich Manipulation
items.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal models have enabled GPT-6 Astra to perform robotic manipulation through in-context learning. Yet contact-rich control and tactile perception are often regarded as strengths of specialist policies, leaving open whether Astra can directly understand and use tactile observations. We provide, to our knowledge, the first demonstration that Astra directly interprets vision-based tactile images and uses their contact cues for manipulation. Tactile RGB images enter through its existing visual interface, enabling few-shot closed-loop control on nineteen simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks with 210 sampled scene seeds per setting. With visuo-tactile input, Astra achieves mean success rates of 93.8% and 81.8%, exceeding the strongest reported specialist baselines in our comparison by 22.9 and 13.1 percentage points, respectively. Vision-only performance also leads these baselines, reaching 76.3% and 80.6%. Trajectory analysis reveals active probing, cautious grasping, contact-guided alignment, and recovery, alongside difficulties with tangential loading and corrective execution. Our findings challenge the exclusivity of specialist policies in contact-rich manipulation and show that fine-grained vision can partially compensate for missing touch. They also identify vision-based tactile sensing as an interface for scaling contact understanding with foundation models and reveal signs of benchmark saturation. These results motivate joint visual-tactile pretraining, harder contact-rich evaluations, and physical-robot validation.

items.title: Guided Diffusion for Trustworthy Synthetic Text Generation
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models is fueled by massive datasets, yet this reliance poses severe privacy risks, as models can inadvertently memorize and even directly output sensitive training data. Synthetic text generation offers a promising solution to this challenge; however, existing methods struggle to reconcile rigorous privacy guarantees with high data utility. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm for private synthetic text generation: Guided Diffusion. Leveraging the unique steerability of Diffusion Language Models, we introduce novel sampling and re-masking procedures that actively guide the iterative denoising steps. These mechanisms steer the generative process to reconstruct fluent text that adheres to a target semantic distribution. We demonstrate that our framework is naturally compatible with Differential Privacy (DP): once the semantic embeddings of the private corpus are protected, the DP guarantee carries over to the generated text by post-processing. Empirically, we show that our approach generates high-quality synthetic text with precise semantic alignment. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness in DP synthetic text generation: across two datasets and two diffusion backbones, it outperforms Private Evolution and DP-SGD-based fine-tuning in distributional fidelity and downstream utility, while generating significantly faster than Private Evolution. We further extend the framework to Data-Specific Indistinguishability (DSI), which adds a formal certificate against data poisoning and memorization at a small utility cost.

items.title: Healthcare Workforce Well-Being Within the Health Promoting Hospitals and Health Services Framework: A Narrative Review and Organizational Case Example
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Healthcare workforce health and well-being are explicitly included within the Health Promoting Hospitals and Health Services (HPH&HS) framework, but the literature has not been synthesized through a dedicated workforce-centered lens. This narrative review examined how workforce health is conceptualized within HPH&HS, operationalized through standards and organizational processes, addressed through workforce-oriented interventions and outcomes, and shaped by organizational conditions influencing implementation. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and CINAHL Complete were searched for publications from 1986 to 2026. Of 323 records identified, 148 were screened after deduplication, 60 full texts were assessed, and 51 reports were included. Evidence was synthesized across four domains: conceptual foundations, standards and governance, workforce interventions and outcomes, and implementation conditions. Results: Workforce health emerged as an intrinsic HPH&HS dimension, with healthcare professionals positioned as both targets and agents of health promotion. Workforce health was increasingly formalized through HPH&HS standards, governance structures, and organizational processes. Leadership, resources, workforce participation, competencies, integration into routine practice, and supportive policy environments emerged as recurrent implementation conditions. Evidence addressed health behaviors, occupational health and safety, psychological well-being, and job satisfaction, as well as organizational culture and staff participation. However, the empirical evidence was predominantly cross-sectional and heterogeneous, with limited controlled or longitudinal research linking HPH&HS implementation to improved workforce health. Conclusions: HPH&HS provides a conceptual and organizational framework for workforce health promotion, but implementation evidence is stronger than evidence for direct and sustained health improvements. Future research should distinguish implementation outcomes, organizational or work-environment indicators, and workforce health outcomes using longitudinal and controlled designs.

items.title: Heart Transplantation: A Review of Recent Advancements in Pre-, Peri, and Post-Transplant Screening and Management
items.abstract: Heart transplantation (HT) remains a critical treatment for patients with end-stage heart failure who remain unresponsive to optimized guideline-directed medical therapy. This review examines recent advancements in pre-, peri-, and post-transplant screening and management aimed at improving patient selection, transplant accessibility, and clinical outcomes. Pre-transplant strategies include comprehensive HT candidate evaluation, risk stratification, donor selection, allocation policies that priotize critically ill patients, and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) to stabilize patients awaiting transplantation. Peri-transplant advances focus on strategies to maintain hemodynamic stability, minimize ischemic injury, and maintain graft viability immediately after HT. Post-transplant management emphasizes individualized immunosuppressive regimens, cardiac allograft rejection surveillance, and the prevention and management of complications to improve graft survival and long-term patient outcomes. Despite substantial progress, significant challenges remain, particularly the shortage of suitable donor organs and the risk of immune-mediated graft rejection. Emerging approaches, including artificial intelligence, xenotransplantation, and regenerative medicine, offer promising opportunities to expand the donor pool, enhance clinical decision-making, and improve HT outcomes. This review examines the research that influences the current policies and practices involved in HT, featuring the pivotal findings as well as any shortcomings present among these studies. Ultimately, continued research and multidisciplinary collaboration in each phase of HT are essential to improve the short and long-term health outcomes of transplant candidates. By integrating established evidence-based practices with emerging technologies, clinicians may further improve equitable access, survival, and quality-of-life for patients with end-stage heart failure.

items.title: Helping in the Situation of Choice: An Empirical Evidence from the Dimensions of Competitive Resources Sharing and Ethno-Cultural Difference
items.abstract: This study examines the evolution of help-giving behaviour among 80 non-governmental organisation (NGO) workers in Ibadan, focusing on factors that influenced their aid provision. The aim is to understand how intrinsic and extrinsic motivations, such as altruism, religious obligations, and organisational values, shaped the help-giving behaviour of NGO workers. A mixed-methods approach was employed, comprising quantitative data collected through surveys and qualitative data obtained from in-depth interviews with NGO leaders and field staff. The quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while thematic analysis was used for the qualitative data. The study found that altruism and religious obligations were the primary motivators for help-giving among NGO workers. These intrinsic motivations were often aligned with personal values and the organisational mission. Cultural values also played a role, although to a lesser extent, while financial incentives were acknowledged but not seen as primary motivators. Overall, intrinsic motivations were more influential than extrinsic rewards in fostering sustained engagement among NGO workers. The findings suggest that NGOs should focus on strengthening intrinsic motivators such as moral responsibility, empathy, and religious or cultural values to maintain staff engagement and commitment, especially during times of financial constraints. This could ensure that workers remain dedicated to their roles and that aid provision remains effective, even when resources are limited.
