items.title: HEROIC: A Research Software Infrastructure for Real-Time Multi-Messenger Observatory Coordination
items.abstract: The era of multi-messenger astronomy, where gravitational waves, electromagnetic radiation, and neutrinos from the same cosmic event must be correlated across a global network of observatories within minutes, presents a fundamental research software engineering challenge: how do you give the astronomical community instant, programmatic situational awareness of thousands of telescopes worldwide? HEROIC (Hop Enabled Realtime Observatory Information and Coordination) is an open-source research software platform developed by the SCIMMA (Scalable Cyberinfrastructure to support Multi-Messenger Astrophysics) project to address precisely this problem. HEROIC provides a REST API and an interactive web interface for tracking telescope status, instrument capabilities, and telescope pointings in real time, across observatories that choose to register with the system. The platform organizes data in a four-level hierarchy (Observatory, Site, Telescope, Instrument) and stores all sky coordinates as PostGIS spatial fields, enabling sub-millisecond spatial queries such as identifying which telescopes have observed (or are planned to observe) a given sky coordinate, using pre-computed field-of-view polygon indexes rather than live geometry calculations. In this talk we present the architecture and design decisions behind HEROIC, with emphasis on the software engineering challenges specific to real-time astronomical coordination: spatial indexing strategies for sky coordinate queries, automated schedule ingestion at cadence, deployment of stateful scientific services on community cloud infrastructure, and the tradeoffs involved in building sustainable open-source tooling for a small but technically diverse scientific community. We also discuss lessons learned from maintaining a production system that bridges telescope control software, public alert brokers, and end-user astronomers, and outline the roadmap for future development including expanded multi-messenger event follow-up coordination features.

items.title: Hidden Signals in Serum Protein Electrophoresis: Artificial Intelligence from Laboratory Pattern Recognition to Clinical Validation
items.abstract: Serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) remains a central laboratory method for the detection and characterization of monoclonal gammopathies and other dysproteinemic patterns. Despite substantial analytical automation, interpretation still relies largely on graphical representation and expert visual assessment, making low-amplitude or borderline abnormalities particularly challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) approaches, has increasingly been applied to SPE, with high performance reported for automated recognition of established abnormalities, particularly M-proteins, i.e., monoclonal immunoglobulins or immunoglobulin fragments produced by clonal plasma cells. However, most models have been developed against predefined diagnostic targets and evaluated using expert interpretation, immunofixation, or immunotyping as reference standards. Improved recognition of known abnormalities should therefore not be equated with discovery of additional clinically meaningful information. Modern electrophoretic platforms generate machine-readable numerical signals that may preserve features not explicitly considered during routine graphical interpretation. This creates the possibility of extending AI-assisted SPE from conventional pattern recognition toward detection of low-amplitude, distributed, or sub-visual signal characteristics. Yet current literature has focused predominantly on algorithmic performance, while the validation pathway required to determine whether additional AI-detected features are biologically meaningful and clinically actionable remains insufficiently defined. Evidence is strongest for automated M-protein recognition, including low-amplitude abnormalities, whereas non-canonical systemic patterns, longitudinal signal analysis, and AI-assisted decomposition of therapeutic monoclonal antibody interference remain exploratory. This critical review addresses this translational gap by evaluating AI applications according to the nature of detected information, strength of supporting evidence, and proximity to clinical implementation. We propose a translational framework addressing four complementary domains: analytical validity, biological validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility. The evidence required in each domain depends on the intended claim and clinical use.

items.title: HOW CAN BEHAVIOURAL AND PSYCHOLOGICAL THEORIES EXPLAIN PATTERNS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) USE AMONG 15-YEAR-OLD STUDENTS, AND HOW ARE THESE PATTERNS ASSOCIATED WITH LEARNING OUTCOMES AND ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE?
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) provides students with rapid access to explanations, summaries, and suggested answers. For 15-year-old learners, this accessibility raises an important educational and behavioural question: under what circumstances does AI support meaningful engagement with challenging learning materials, and when might it reduce opportunities for independent cognitive effort? This paper reviews published research in behavioural science and selected findings from the OECD's PISA 2025 Results (Volume I), with particular emphasis on Uzbekistan. Cognitive-demand avoidance and cognitive offloading are employed as theoretical frameworks for interpreting patterns of AI use, while a clear distinction is maintained between these concepts and the variables directly measured by PISA. According to the OECD, 48.6% of students in Uzbekistan use AI chatbots at least once a week to support their learning, compared with the OECD average of 45.5%. Furthermore, 80.6% of students in Uzbekistan report learning at school how to evaluate AI-generated information, compared with an OECD average of 62.6% (OECD, 2026). These findings indicate that AI-assisted learning is already widespread among students. However, the reported figures do not establish how frequently students substitute AI-generated summaries for assigned reading materials or identify the motivations underlying individual decisions to use AI in this way. The paper argues that the educational implications of AI use depend on the nature of the cognitive tasks delegated to AI, the learner's objectives, and the extent to which AI-generated information is critically evaluated and integrated into independent learning. As the study relies on secondary sources and does not involve the analysis of individual-level student records or the collection of primary empirical data, the proposed explanations should be understood as theoretically informed interpretations rather than established causal relationships. The paper concludes that educational institutions should develop students' ability not only to use AI tools effectively but also to recognise when independent reading, source verification, and critical reasoning remain essential for meaningful learning.

items.title: How Effectively Do Security Skills Guide Coding Agents in Vulnerability Detection in Linux Kernel?
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Claude Code, are increasingly used for security auditing, with task-specific skills providing reusable vulnerability-analysis procedures. However, their effectiveness in detecting real vulnerabilities and the reasons for their failures remain unclear. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 37 security skills using Claude Code with four underlying LLMs on 100 real Linux kernel vulnerabilities across ten classes, totaling 14800 runs. We evaluate vulnerability detection at the function, statement, and vulnerability-class levels. Results show that 24.4 percent of runs locate the correct function, 18.3 percent identify both the function and responsible statement, and 15.7 percent correctly classify the vulnerability. Our failure analysis reveals limitations in evidence acquisition, state-relation reasoning, code interpretation, candidate verification, investigation coverage, and reporting. Based on these findings, we propose SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that iteratively evolves security skills by learning from missed vulnerabilities and failure patterns. We evolve five top-performing skills using the original benchmark and evaluate them on 100 previously unseen vulnerabilities. SKILL-SIF improves fully correct vulnerability detection by up to eight times (from 2 percent to 16 percent) on unseen vulnerabilities, while aggregate accuracy across four LLMs increases by 1.85 times (from 6.05 percent to 11.20 percent). These findings highlight the limitations of existing security skills and demonstrate the potential of failure-driven skill evolution to improve vulnerability detection in coding agents.

items.title: Human Factors in AI-Assisted Interpreter Training: A Design Science Approach to Human-Centred Educational Technology
items.abstract: The educational value of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on technological capabilities and human–AI interaction. This is particularly relevant in interpreter training, which involves high cognitive demands, contextual decisions, and time-sensitive activities. This study examines how Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI) principles can guide AI-assisted educational environments for interpreter training. Using Design Science Research (DSR), an environment integrating AI capabilities across the training cycle was developed and evaluated. Drawing on literature concerning Computer-Assisted Interpreting, HCAI, human–AI interaction, technology acceptance, and interpreting cognition, five design principles were derived: learner agency and human control, transparency and calibrated trust, protection of cognitive resources, contextualised assistance, and AI as a support for learning. A technology acceptance study involving 42 professional interpreters provided contextual evidence on technology use, adoption barriers, and professional practice, informing the specification of these principles. The principles were operationalised in the artefact, and its interaction design was examined through formative heuristic evaluation. Professional evidence therefore informs the design without establishing learner-centred validation or educational effectiveness. The contribution is a human-centred, professionally informed framework linking literature, contextual evidence, design requirements, and implementation to align AI capabilities with educational objectives and the cognitive and interactional demands of interpreter training through explicit and traceable design decisions.
